p.src: That night, Zhang Liao shot Huang Gai into the water with an arrow, then helped Cao Cao ashore. By the time they found horses and fled, the army was already in utter disorder. Han Dang charged through smoke and flame to attack the naval stockade, when a soldier suddenly reported, “There is a man at the stern rudder calling out Your Excellency’s courtesy name!” Han Dang listened carefully and heard the man cry, “Yigong, save me!” Han Dang said, “That is Huang Gongfu!” He hastily ordered that Huang Gai be rescued. They saw that Huang Gai had been wounded by an arrow. He had bitten off the shaft, but the arrowhead remained buried in his flesh. Han Dang quickly stripped off his wet clothes, cut out the arrowhead with a knife, and bound the wound with a torn banner. He then gave Huang Gai his own battle robe to wear and had another boat take him back to the main camp for treatment. As it happened, Huang Gai was an excellent swimmer; thus, though he had fallen into the river in armor amid the bitter cold, he escaped with his life.

p.src: That day, flames surged across the whole river, while battle cries shook the earth. On the left, the forces of Han Dang and Jiang Qin attacked from west of Red Cliffs; on the right, the forces of Zhou Tai and Chen Wu attacked from east of Red Cliffs; and in the center came the great fleet of Zhou Yu, Cheng Pu, Xu Sheng, and Ding Feng. The fire answered the troops, and the troops drew might from the fire. This indeed was: battle upon the waters of the Three Rivers, fierce war at Red Cliffs. p.src: But let us leave the fierce fighting on the river. Gan Ning had Cai Zhong lead him deep into Cao Cao’s camp; there he cut Cai Zhong down from his horse with a single stroke and set fire to the grass. Seeing flames rise from the central camp in the distance, Lü Meng also started fires in more than ten places to support Gan Ning. Pan Zhang and Dong Xi split up, setting fires and shouting battle cries. All around, the thunder of drums rose deafeningly. Cao Cao and Zhang Liao led more than a hundred horsemen through a forest of flames, but wherever they looked ahead, everything was burning. As they fled, Mao Jie arrived with Wen Ping, whom he had rescued, and some ten horsemen. Cao Cao ordered the soldiers to find a way out. Zhang Liao pointed and said, “Only Wulin offers open ground through which we can escape.” Cao Cao headed straight for Wulin.

p.src: As they fled, a force caught up from behind, shouting, “Cao Cao, you traitor, do not flee!” In the firelight appeared Lü Meng’s banners. Cao Cao urged his men and horses onward, leaving Zhang Liao to hold the rear against Lü Meng. Then more torches flared ahead, and an army poured from a mountain valley, shouting, “Ling Tong is here!” Cao Cao was terrified out of his wits. Suddenly, another force came charging obliquely from the side, crying, “Prime Minister, do not be alarmed! Xu Huang is here!” After a confused melee, they fought open a road and fled north. Suddenly they saw a body of troops stationed before a hillside. Xu Huang rode out to question them. They proved to be Ma Yan and Zhang Zi, former officers of Yuan Shao who had surrendered, encamped there with three thousand northern troops; seeing flames fill the sky that night, they had not dared to move, and thus happened to meet Cao Cao. Cao Cao ordered the two generals to lead a thousand troops ahead to clear the way, while the rest remained to guard him. With these fresh troops at his disposal, Cao Cao felt somewhat reassured. Ma Yan and Zhang Zi galloped ahead. Before they had gone ten li, a battle cry arose and a force appeared. The general at their head shouted, “I am Gan Xingba of Eastern Wu!” Ma Yan was about to engage him when Gan Ning cut him down from his horse with a single stroke. Zhang Zi leveled his spear and came to meet him. Gan Ning gave a mighty shout, and before Zhang Zi could react, Gan Ning struck with his blade and sent him tumbling from his horse. The rear ranks hastened to report this to Cao Cao. Cao Cao was then counting on reinforcements from Hefei. But Sun Quan was at the road to Hefei; seeing the firelight on the river and knowing his army had won, he ordered Lu Xun to kindle a signal fire. When Taishi Ci saw it, he joined forces with Lu Xun and charged forward. Cao Cao had no choice but to flee toward Yiling. On the road he encountered Zhang He and ordered him to guard the rear.

p.src: Spurring their horses onward, they fled until the fifth watch. Looking back and seeing the glow of the fires gradually recede, Cao Cao at last felt at ease and asked, “What place is this?” Those around him replied, “This is west of Wulin and north of Yidu.” Seeing the tangled woods and rugged mountains and rivers, Cao Cao threw back his head on horseback and laughed without cease. The generals asked, “Why does the Prime Minister laugh?” Cao Cao said, “I am laughing at no one but Zhou Yu for his lack of strategy and Zhuge Liang for his want of wisdom. Had I been directing the campaign, I would have stationed an ambush here beforehand. What then would we have done?”

p.src: Before he had finished speaking, drums thundered on both sides and flames soared into the sky, startling Cao Cao so badly that he nearly fell from his horse. A force charged out obliquely from the side, shouting, “I, Zhao Zilong, have awaited you here a long while by order of the Military Adviser!” Cao Cao ordered Xu Huang and Zhang He to fight Zhao Yun together, while he himself fled through smoke and flame. Zilong did not pursue him, but devoted himself to seizing banners, and so Cao Cao escaped.

p.src: Dawn was just breaking; black clouds shrouded the earth, and the southeast wind still had not ceased. Suddenly, rain poured down in torrents, soaking clothes and armor through. Cao Cao and his soldiers pressed on through the rain, and hunger showed on every face. Cao Cao ordered the soldiers to plunder food from the villages and search for kindling. Just as they were about to cook, another force caught up from behind. Cao Cao was greatly alarmed. But it proved to be Li Dian and Xu Chu, escorting the assembled advisers.

p.src: Cao Cao was delighted. He ordered the troops to continue onward and asked, “What place lies ahead?” A man reported, “One road is the main road to South Yiling; the other is the mountain road to North Yiling.” Cao Cao asked, “Which way is shorter to Nan Commandery and Jiangling?” A soldier replied, “The easiest way is through South Yiling and then by Hulu Pass.” Cao Cao ordered them to take the road to South Yiling. When they reached Hulu Pass, all the soldiers were so famished they could scarcely walk. The horses too were exhausted, and many collapsed on the road. Cao Cao ordered the troops ahead to halt for a while. Some had brought cooking pots on their horses, while others had plundered grain from villages. They chose dry ground beside the mountain, set up the pots, and cooked rice; they cut up horseflesh and roasted it to eat. All stripped off their wet clothes and spread them where the wind could dry them. The horses were unsaddled and released to graze, gnawing at grass roots.

p.src: Cao Cao sat beneath the sparse trees, threw back his head, and laughed loudly. The officers asked, “A moment ago, Prime Minister, you laughed at Zhou Yu and Zhuge Liang, only to bring Zhao Zilong upon us and lose many men and horses. Why do you laugh again now?” Cao Cao said, “I laugh because Zhuge Liang and Zhou Yu are, after all, deficient in strategy. Had I been commanding, I would have planted an ambush right here, letting fresh troops await their weary foe. Even if we escaped with our lives, we could not avoid grievous losses. They failed to foresee this, and that is why I laugh.”

p.src: While he was still speaking, the troops both ahead and behind raised a battle cry together. Cao Cao was greatly startled; he cast off his armor and mounted his horse. Many of the soldiers had no time even to retrieve their horses. Already smoke and fire closed around the mountain pass on every side, and an army deployed before them. At its head was Zhang Yide of Yan, sitting his horse with spear held crosswise. He shouted, “Cao Cao, you traitor! Where do you think you are going?” At the sight of Zhang Fei, every soldier and general was struck with terror. Xu Chu rode an unsaddled horse to fight Zhang Fei. Zhang Liao and Xu Huang also spurred forward to attack him from both sides. The forces on both sides became entangled in a confused melee. Cao Cao was the first to wheel his horse and escape, while his generals each fought their own way free. Zhang Fei pursued them from behind. Cao Cao fled on and on. When the pursuers had gradually fallen behind, he looked back and saw that many of his generals were wounded.

p.src: As they marched on, a soldier reported, “There are two roads ahead. Which one does the丞相 wish to take?” Cao Cao asked, “Which road is shorter?” The soldier replied, “The main road is somewhat level, but it is over fifty li longer; the narrow road leads through the Huarong Pass and is over fifty li shorter. But the ground is confined, the road treacherous, and its pits and hollows make travel difficult.” Cao Cao sent men up a hill to reconnoiter. They returned and reported, “Smoke is rising from several places beside the narrow road. There is no movement at all on the main road.” Cao Cao ordered the vanguard to take the narrow road through Huarong. His officers said, “Where beacon smoke rises, troops must surely be waiting. Why take that road instead?” Cao Cao replied, “Have you not heard the military maxim: ‘Where there is emptiness, make it seem substantial; where there is substance, make it seem empty’? Zhuge Liang is full of schemes. He has therefore had smoke lit in that remote mountain country to deter us from taking this road, while he waits in ambush on the main road. I have seen through his plan, and I refuse to fall into his trap!” The officers all said, “The丞相’s wondrous foresight is beyond all others.” They therefore marshaled the troops and took the Huarong road. By then the men were collapsing from hunger and all the horses were exhausted. Those with scorched heads and blistered faces hobbled along with support, while those struck by arrows or spears forced themselves onward. Their clothes and armor were soaked through, and not one man’s equipment was whole; weapons, banners, and pennants were all in disorder. Most had been driven into such panic on the Yiling road that they rode bare-backed horses, having thrown away saddles, bridles, and clothing alike. It was the bitter cold of midwinter; their suffering was beyond description.

p.src: Seeing the vanguard halt and refuse to advance, Cao Cao asked the reason. The reply came: “The mountain road ahead is narrow and remote. This morning’s rain has filled the pits and ditches with standing water, and the mud swallows the horses’ hooves, so we cannot advance.” Cao Cao flew into a rage and shouted, “An army cuts a road when it meets a mountain and builds a bridge when it meets water. How can mere mud make a road impassable?” He issued an order that the old, the weak, and the wounded should follow slowly in the rear, while the strong carried earth, bound firewood, and hauled grass and reeds to fill the road, so that the army might move at once; whoever disobeyed would be beheaded. The soldiers had no choice but to dismount, cut bamboo and timber beside the road, and use them to fill the mountain track. Fearing pursuit from the rear, Cao Cao ordered Zhang Liao, Xu Chu, and Xu Huang to lead a hundred horsemen with drawn blades and behead anyone who lagged.

p.src: Cao Cao shouted for men and horses to proceed along the plankways, and the dead were beyond counting. The sound of wailing never ceased along the road. Cao Cao said angrily, “Life and death are decreed by fate. What is there to weep over? Anyone who weeps again will be beheaded on the spot!” Of every three parts of the men and horses, one fell behind, one filled the gullies, and only one followed Cao Cao. Once they passed the worst of the peril, the road became somewhat level. Cao Cao looked back and saw only a little over three hundred horsemen behind him, not one with clothes and armor in proper order. Cao Cao urged them to hasten onward. The officers said, “The horses are utterly spent. We must rest a little.” Cao Cao replied, “It will not be too late to rest once we reach Jingzhou.” They had gone less than a few more li when Cao Cao raised his whip in the saddle and laughed aloud. The officers asked, “Why does the丞相 laugh again?” Cao Cao said, “Everyone claims that Zhou Yu and Zhuge Liang are resourceful men of great wisdom. As I see it, they are inept after all. Had they placed even one brigade in ambush here, we would all have been captured without resistance.”

p.src: Before he had finished speaking, a cannon boomed. Five hundred broadsword guards deployed on both sides, and at their head stood the great general Guan Yunchang, gripping the Green Dragon Blade and mounted on the Red Hare, barring the road. At the sight, Cao Cao’s troops were terrified out of their wits and stared helplessly at one another. Cao Cao said, “Now that we have come to this, we can only fight to the death!” The officers replied, “Even if the men are not afraid, the horses have no strength left. How can we fight again?” Cheng Yu said, “I have long known Yunchang to be haughty toward his superiors yet compassionate toward those beneath him, to challenge the strong but never oppress the weak. He distinguishes gratitude from grievance and has always been renowned for honor and fidelity. The丞相 once showed him kindness. If you appeal to him in person now, we may escape this danger.”

p.src: Cao Cao followed his advice, spurred forward, bowed slightly from the saddle, and said to Yunchang, “General, have you been well since we parted?” Yunchang also inclined his body and replied, “I, Guan, have received the military adviser’s orders and have long been waiting for the丞相.” Cao Cao said, “My army is defeated and my position desperate. I have reached this place with no road left to me. I pray you, General, give weight to our former friendship.” Yunchang replied, “Though I once received the丞相’s generous favor, I repaid it by slaying Yan Liang and Wen Chou and lifting the siege of Baima. How could I now neglect public duty for private feeling?” Cao Cao said, “Do you still remember when you slew my generals at the five passes? A true man holds honor and fidelity above all. You understand the Spring and Autumn Annals profoundly. Surely you know the story of Yu Gongzhisi pursuing Zizhuo Ruzi?”

Remembering Cao Cao’s many past kindnesses and what had later happened when he slew the generals at the five passes, how could his heart remain unmoved? Then he saw Cao Cao’s troops trembling in distress, all on the verge of tears, and his heart softened further. He therefore reined his horse around and told his troops, “Spread out to either side.” This was plainly meant to let Cao Cao escape. Seeing Yunchang turn his horse, Cao Cao and his officers charged past together. By the time Yunchang turned back, Cao Cao and his officers had already passed. While he hesitated, Zhang Liao came galloping up. At the sight of him, Yunchang’s affection for an old friend was stirred anew;
with a long sigh, he let them all go. A later poet wrote:

p.src: Having escaped the peril at Huarong, Cao Cao reached the mouth of a valley and looked back. Only twenty-seven horsemen remained with him. By nightfall they were nearing Nanjun when a blaze of torches appeared and a body of troops blocked the road. Cao Cao cried in alarm, “My life is ended!” A troop of scouts charged up, and only then did he recognize them as Cao Ren’s men. Only then was Cao Cao’s mind at ease. Cao Ren received him, saying, “Though I knew the army had been defeated, I dared not go far away and could only remain nearby to meet you.” Cao Cao said, “I came within a hair of never seeing you again!”

p.src: He then led everyone into Nanjun to rest. Zhang Liao arrived afterward and told of Yunchang’s benevolence. Cao Cao mustered his officers and found that very many were wounded, so he ordered them all to recuperate. Cao Ren prepared wine to dispel Cao Cao’s gloom, and all the strategists attended the feast. Suddenly Cao Cao raised his face to heaven and wept bitterly. The strategists said, “While escaping from the tiger’s den, the丞相 showed no fear at all. Now we have reached the city, the men have eaten, and the horses have fodder. This is the time to reorder the army and avenge our defeat. Why do you instead weep so bitterly?” Cao Cao replied, “I weep for Guo Fengxiao! Had Fengxiao been alive, he would never have allowed me to suffer so great a defeat!” He beat his breast and wailed, “Alas, Fengxiao! What anguish, Fengxiao! What a loss, Fengxiao!” All the strategists fell silent, ashamed of themselves.

p.src: The next day, Cao Cao summoned Cao Ren and said, “I shall now return temporarily to the capital at Xu, assemble my forces, and surely return to avenge this defeat. You must preserve Nanjun intact. I shall leave a secret plan here. Do not open it unless the need is urgent; when an emergency comes, open it. Follow the plan, and Eastern Wu will not dare look Nanjun in the face.” Cao Ren asked, “Who should defend Hefei and Xiangyang?” Cao Cao replied, “I entrust Jingzhou to your command; I have already assigned Xiahou Dun to guard Xiangyang. Hefei is the most vital position. I have appointed Zhang Liao chief commander, with Yue Jin and Li Dian as his deputies, to defend it. If any emergency arises, send me a swift report.”

p.src: Having completed his dispositions, Cao Cao mounted and led his followers back toward Xuchang. All the civil and military officials of Jingzhou who had originally surrendered were taken back to Xuchang as before, to be assigned new duties. Cao Ren for his part sent Cao Hong to hold Yiling and Nanjun against Zhou Yu.

p.src: Now Guan Yunzhang, having let Cao Cao go, led his troops back. By then, the armies from all the other routes had returned to Xiakou with captured horses, weapons, money, and provisions; Yunzhang alone had captured neither a man nor a horse and returned empty-handed to see Xuande. Kongming was congratulating Xuande when word suddenly came that Yunzhang had arrived. Kongming hastily left his seat and went to welcome him, cup in hand, saying, “Let us rejoice that the general has performed this peerless deed and rid the whole realm of a great scourge. This surely deserves a grand celebration.”

p.src: Yunzhang remained silent. Kongming said, “Can it be that the general is displeased because we did not go far out to welcome you?” Turning to those around him, he said, “Why did none of you report his arrival sooner?” Yunzhang said, “I, Guan, have come expressly to ask for death.” Kongming said, “Did Cao Cao perhaps fail to come by the Huarong Road?” Yunzhang said, “He did come that way. But I proved incapable and allowed him to escape.” Kongming said, “Which of his officers and soldiers did you capture?” Yunzhang said, “I captured none of them.” Kongming said, “Yunzhang must have remembered the kindness Cao Cao once showed him and deliberately let him go. But since his written pledge to obey the military order is here, I cannot but enforce military law.” He then ordered the guards to take Yunzhang out and behead him. Just so:
